Okay, the user wants multiplayer support with a lobby and also wants performance optimizations because the game is running slowly. I’ve already added a WebSocket server (server.js), a client networking module (net.js), and a shared soldier model (soldier.js) that can be used by both bots and remote players. The next logical piece is to implement the enemy AI logic that will run on the host (or in solo mode) and be represented to other clients via a proxy.

I need to create a new source file under the src directory for the enemy AI. Looking at the existing codebase, there is already a player controller (probably in player.js) that handles movement, aiming, shooting, etc. The enemy AI should mirror much of that functionality but be driven by a state machine rather than direct input. It should also integrate with the networking layer: the host will simulate bots and broadcast their state, while remote clients will receive updates and render BotProxy objects.

First, I need to import Three.js and the shared soldier builder from soldier.js. The enemy class will need constants for the various bot states: PATROL, ALERT, COMBAT, HUNT, DEAD. I’ll define an exported BOT_STATE object for external reference.

The AI will need raycasting for vision checks, so I’ll create reusable Raycaster, Vector3, and forward direction vectors as module-level variables to avoid reallocating them each frame.

The Enemy class constructor should accept the scene, a spawn definition (including position and waypoints), and a unique id. Inside, I’ll set up basic properties: id, scene reference, initial state (PATROL), health, waypoints (converted to THREE.Vector3), waypoint index, random initial yaw, timers for vision, reaction, lose-sight, burst fire, etc. I also need to create a THREE.Group to hold the model, position it at the spawn location, build the soldier parts using buildSoldier (passing the group and a “hostile” palette), store references to hitboxes, head, muzzle, legs for later use, and add the group to the scene. Also tag hitboxes with a reference to the enemy for collision detection.

I’ll add getters for position, alive status, and head world position (used for vision). The netState method will return a compact array of the enemy’s id, x, z, yaw, state, and hp – this is what will be sent over the network.

Vision logic: a canSee method that takes a target eye position, the solids (static geometry), and optionally performs an FOV check. It calculates direction, distance, early-outs if beyond 30 units, normalizes, checks FOV by comparing dot product with a forward vector derived from yaw (model faces -Z at yaw 0). Then uses the raycaster to test for occlusion against the solids’ children, returning true if no obstruction.

Target selection: pickTarget iterates over ctx.targets (which are player objects with id, eye, pos) and selects the closest one that is visible (using canSee). getTarget simply finds the current target by id.

A hearGunshot method for reacting to nearby gunfire when patrolling.

takeDamage reduces hp, handles death (setting state to DEAD, resetting death timer), and if still alive, switches to COMBAT state with a reaction delay.

Movement helpers: faceToward sets targetYaw based on a direction vector; moveToward moves towards a target point with speed, handling collisions via a collides method that checks against an array of bounding boxes (colliders). collides does a simple capsule check.

animateLegs will swing the leg meshes based on time and speed.

The update method drives the state machine each frame (dt). If dead, run a death animation (fall over). Otherwise, smooth turn towards targetYaw, update yaw, set group rotation. Vision runs at 8 Hz (0.125 sec interval). Depending on state, it either patrols waypoints, looks for targets, reacts, engages in combat (including firing via combatFire), hunts last known positions, etc. The combatFire method handles burst fire logic, random hit calculation, and calls ctx.botFire to inform the host of a shot.

Finally, a dispose method to clean up the group from the scene.

All of this matches the architecture used elsewhere (player.js) and will integrate with net.js (which will broadcast the netState). I should write this as a single file enemy.js under src. The content must be exactly as drafted, with proper imports, exported BOT_STATE, class definition, and all methods. I’ll use template literals to embed the code verbatim.

Now I’ll issue a Write tool call to create D:\fps\src\enemy.js with the full content I just designed.
